items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president.

ctx.x: I had no thoughts at that time of becoming in any way professionally involved in the music, but I was — it was like 52nd Street was in its final stages, but it was still alive and it was no small thing to have Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s and across the street maybe Charlie Parker if you were lucky and he was in town. And, you know, Billie Holiday at the Onyx Club. So there was still a lot going on. And this was, you know, still a vibrant time. There was downtown on weekends, there was the Stuyvesant Casino in…

not much more than a glorified messenger but I got to meet a lot of people and actually was talked into running for office at the American Newspaper Guild, a pretty left wing thing. I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president. That was that famous election when Truman — Truman and Dewey. And it was a great experience because I was working at Time Inc. I was at a nerve center there on election night, which was a studio where they were broadcasting, and there was a guy named H.V. Kaltenborn, who was —…

downstairs called Mahogany Hall, which was the traditional club, and upstairs was Storyville, and on Sunday afternoons both bands would play. And then at the end there would be some get-together. So the most remarkable thing that involved that kind of a Sunday afternoon was when Art Tatum’s trio was upstairs and Sidney Bechet was downstairs. And for the jam they got together and played as Sidney sat in with the Tatum trio, and they played “Lady Be Good” and that was a [gestures]. This was on the occasion — that…

items.q: Anyway, I got involved with the Progressive Party, rang doorbells for Henry Wallace, and went to a couple of meetings, at one of which there was the guest speaker – it’s a

ctx.x: absolutely delighted with that. Probably that was about the closest we came at that point. It was like I had done something that – it’s not as if, when I started to write and when I became editor of magazines, yes, he said nice things, and he was proud of me in a way, but that accomplishment – I’m glad that he lived to see that. He unfortunately did not live very long after Adam was born. Anyway, he said, “No, no, no, no Hollywood,” but he did hook me up. He had somebody who knew somebody at what was called the…

like being a college sophomore, a little bit like that. I couldn’t stand this pap. I just left after three weeks. I left. It was terrible. The only thing I was interested in was American. So I went to night school. I went to Washington Irving down on 14th Street. They had a thing where you could take a course in American history. I wanted to learn something about that, because I was pretty blank on that. Anyway, he sent me to this nice man at the March of Time. He said to me, “There is something” – we are now in…

very informal – not too many people – was a young writer who had just published his first novel, named Norman Mailer, but I can’t say that he was a very nice guy, even then. He was huffy. That’s in my opinion the only good book that he ever wrote. The Naked and the Dead is a very good novel, and he’ll probably – I think his reputation will rest on that. Everything else you can forget about, especially what he’s doing now, writing about Hitler. He couldn’t find anything better to do. That’s enough of that. Part of…
